To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 5-lipoxygenase (5-LO) pathway metabolite hepoxilin A. is a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils and monocytes and is a key mediator of the inflammatory response to bacterial infection.

the lipoxygenase-derived lipid mediator hepoxilin A3 facilitates neutrophil recruitment into the lungs during P. aeruginosa pneumonia by promoting adhesion of neutrophils to endothelial cells, and that hepoxilin A is produced by airway epithelial cells and is a novel target for anti-infective therapy.

the neutrophilic breach of epithelial barriers is a key event in the pathogenesis of pneumonia and that the neutrophils use a novel pathway involving 12/15-LOX, 12- and 15-HETEs, and hepoxilin A3 to breach the epithelial barrier and gain access to the submucosal tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the lipoxygenase pathway in the regulation of innate and adaptive immunity.
the role of 12-lipoxygenase in the regulation of neutrophilic inflammation in airway epithelial cells.
understanding the role of lipoxygenase-derived eicosanoids in the regulation of the innate immune response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lipoxygenases, in the presence of the appropriate substrates and under specific conditions, can generate bioactive products with the capacity to modulate the immune response.

neutrophils are not the only cells that can breach the airway epithelium and that the epithelium is a complex structure that is not only capable of being breached, but also of being breached in different ways, and that these breaches can be facilitated by different mechanisms.
